A real cell has resistance inside it — what does the voltmeter read as R falls?

Listen to the intro

About: Terminal Voltage vs. Load — The Sagging Battery

Concept

A real battery is modelled as an ideal EMF source ε in series with a small internal resistance r. When a load R draws current I, the voltmeter reads the terminal voltage V = ε − Ir. As the load stiffens (smaller R, larger I), the internal drop grows and the measured voltage sags below the nameplate EMF.

What you can do

EMF ε
Set the ideal source voltage (1.0–12.0 V).
Internal resistance r
Vary the battery's hidden drop (0.05–5.0 Ω).
Load R
Dial the external resistance on a logarithmic scale, 0.1 Ω (near-short) to 1.0 kΩ (near open circuit).
Readouts
Current I, terminal voltage V, internal drop Ir, and power delivered.

Guided Inquiry

1 · A real cell

A real cell is an ideal source of EMF ε in series with its own internal resistance r, both inside the dashed box. A load R across the terminals carries a current I, and the voltmeter reads the terminal voltage V.

Here ε = 9.00 V, r = 0.50 Ω and R = 100 Ω.

2 · Lowering the load

The load is lowered from R = 100 Ω to R = 1 Ω, so the current through the cell rises. What happens to the terminal voltage V?

3 · Where the volts went

Lower the load from R = 100 Ω to R = 1 Ω. Of the three heights in the voltage column — the EMF ε, the internal drop Ir and the terminal voltage V — which one does not move, and which two trade against each other?

4 · Reading the full EMF

Under what condition does the voltmeter read (very nearly) the full EMF ε?

5 · A tired cell, shorted

This cell has aged: r is now 3.00 Ω, and at R = 1.00 Ω the terminals hold only 2.25 V. Its terminals are now joined by a wire of negligible resistance, so R → 0. What sets the current that flows?

Terminal Voltage vs. Load

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A real battery is not a perfect source of voltage, because its own material resists the charge it pushes. The sim wires one real cell to a load resistor, with an ammeter in the loop and a voltmeter across the terminals.

What you'll learn

  • What the EMF ε and the internal resistance r of a real cell mean.
  • How the current depends on ε, r and the load R.
  • What a voltmeter across the terminals reads, compared with ε.
The cell (ε and r in the dashed box), the load R, an ammeter and a voltmeter.

What's on screen

  • EMF ε: the amber plates and the amber column.
  • Internal resistance r: the red zigzag in the dashed box, and the red part (Ir) of a column.
  • Voltmeter: the green circle with its reading, and the green part (V) of a column.
  • Load R: the zigzag on the right wire. Teal dots circulate, and the ammeter A shows I.
  • Voltage bars (fixed 0 to 14 V axis) and the Live readouts panel.
See itPress Play at the opening values. Watch for: teal dots circulating through the ammeter, the load and the cell.

Dot count and speed follow the logarithm of I, so the whole range stays visible. Read the number, not the dots. Fixed: both meters are ideal, so the voltmeter draws no current, and ε and r stay constant as the current changes.

03

The current is the EMF divided by the total resistance

The loop has one path. The charge must pass through the load R and also through the cell's own resistance r, so the two resistances are in series and add. The EMF drives the current through their sum:

I = ε / (R + r)
I in amperes, ε in volts, R and r in ohms. The same I flows through the cell and the load.

With ε = 9.00 V and r = 0.50 Ω the table follows from this one formula. A load of 100 Ω gives only 0.09 A, and the current grows as the load shrinks.

RR + rI = 9.00 V / (R + r)
100 Ω100.50 Ω0.09 A
10 Ω10.50 Ω0.86 A
1 Ω1.50 Ω6.00 A
0.1 Ω0.60 Ω15.00 A
See itPlay the opening values, with R = 1.00 Ω. Watch for: I = 6.00 A on the ammeter, which is 9.00 / (1.00 + 0.50).
04

The terminal voltage is the EMF minus the drop across r

The current I crosses the internal resistance r, so by Ohm's law a voltage Ir is lost inside the cell. Going once round the loop, the EMF is shared between that drop and the load:

ε = Ir + IR   ⇒   V = ε − Ir = IR
V is the terminal voltage, the reading of the voltmeter across the cell.

At the opening values I = 6.00 A, so Ir = 6.00 × 0.50 = 3.00 V. The voltmeter reads V = 9.00 − 3.00 = 6.00 V, which also equals IR = 6.00 × 1.00. The second bar column is built from exactly these two parts, a red Ir segment on a green V segment, and its total height is the amber ε column.

See itPlay the opening values and compare the two columns. Watch for: V = 6.00 V and Ir = 3.00 V, stacked to the height of the 9.00 V column.
05

A light load leaves the terminal voltage close to the EMF

Eliminating I gives V = εR/(R + r), so the fraction of the EMF that reaches the terminals is R/(R + r). It depends only on the ratio of R to r. When R is much larger than r, the current is small, Ir is negligible, and V is very nearly ε.

R (r = 0.50 Ω)V / εV at ε = 9.00 V
100 Ω99.5 %8.96 V
10 Ω95.2 %8.57 V
1 Ω66.7 %6.00 V
0.5 Ω50.0 %4.50 V
0.1 Ω16.7 %1.50 V

In the limit of no load, with no current at all, V equals ε exactly. This is why a high-resistance voltmeter on a cell standing alone reads its full EMF. Doubling ε at a fixed load doubles I, Ir and V together, and leaves the fraction unchanged.

ε r R

These sliders move the sim too.

See itRaise the load to R = 100 Ω. Watch for: the green part of the second column nearly as tall as the amber one, with V = 8.96 V and Ir = 0.04 V.
06

A short circuit is limited only by the internal resistance

As R falls towards zero, R + r tends to r. The current then tends to its largest possible value, and the terminal voltage tends to zero:

R → 0   ⇒   I → ε / r,   V → 0
A wire across the terminals leaves only r in the loop.

The opening cell could give up to 9.00 / 0.50 = 18.0 A. At the lowest load in the sim, 0.1 Ω, it gives 15.00 A and V = 1.50 V. A worn cell has a larger r. With r = 3.00 Ω, ε / r is only 3.00 A. At R = 0.1 Ω that cell gives 2.90 A and V = 0.29 V. The cell also heats at I²r. At 15 A that is 112.5 W, five times the 22.5 W in the load. The sim does not display it.

See itSet r to 3.00 Ω and lower the load to its minimum, 0.1 Ω. Watch for: I = 2.90 A and the green part of the column nearly gone, V = 0.29 V.
07

The load receives the most power when R equals r

The load receives P = I²R = ε²R/(R + r)². A large R gives a small current, and a small R gives a small voltage across the load, so P is small at both ends. Setting dP/dR = 0 puts the maximum at R = r. There V = ε/2 and P = ε²/4r.

R (ε = 9.00 V, r = 0.50 Ω)P = I²R
0.1 Ω22.50 W
0.5 Ω40.50 W
1 Ω36.00 W
2 Ω25.92 W

The largest power, 81/(4 × 0.5) = 40.5 W, is delivered when R = 0.50 Ω. The cell then spends as much power inside itself as in the load, so only half of the total εI reaches the load.

See itMove the load to about 0.5 Ω, where R matches r. Watch for: Power to load peaking at about 40.50 W, with V near half of ε.
08

Where it matters

  • Measuring ε and r. V = ε − Ir is a straight line when V is plotted against I, with intercept ε and slope −r. Two readings are enough. From (6.00 V, 6.00 A) and (8.96 V, 0.09 A), r = (8.96 − 6.00)/(6.00 − 0.09) = 0.50 Ω and ε = 6.00 + 6.00 × 0.50 = 9.00 V.
  • Reading the EMF. A voltmeter of very large resistance draws almost no current, so it reads very nearly ε. A low-resistance meter would sag the reading.
  • Heavy loads. A device that draws a large current, such as a starter motor, lowers the terminal voltage of its battery, and the lights on the same battery dim.
  • Tired cells. An old cell can read close to its full EMF with no load, yet collapse under a real load, because its r has grown.
09

Summary

In one line. A real cell behaves like an ideal source of EMF ε in series with an internal resistance r, and the load R shares the loop with r.

Key points

  • I = ε/(R + r), and ε = Ir + IR.
  • V = ε − Ir = εR/(R + r). V → ε when R ≫ r.
  • Shorted, R → 0: I → ε/r and V → 0.
  • The load power is largest at R = r, equal to ε²/4r.

Common mix-ups

  • "The terminal voltage always equals the EMF." Only with no current. Otherwise V = ε − Ir.
  • "A shorted cell gives an unlimited current." It is limited to ε/r.
  • "The most power also means the best efficiency." At R = r only half the power reaches the load.

Things to try on your own

  • Set ε = 9.0 V, r = 1.00 Ω and R = 1.00 Ω, and predict V (4.50 V) before you read it.
  • At R = 1.00 Ω, raise ε from 6.0 V to 12.0 V and check that I, Ir and V all double.
  • At R = 1.00 Ω, raise r from 0.50 Ω to 3.00 Ω and watch V fall to 2.25 V.
